text.en:
Forty students shouted out idli, dosa, pongal or poori all at once.
"Hold on—let's use tally marks and a graph so everyone can see the winner cleanly!" said Dev.

Data is a collection of facts or numbers gathered to answer a question. Organising raw lists with tally marks—bundling groups of five with a diagonal slash—gives a neat frequency table.
A pictograph shows data using repeating pictures or symbols, each worth a chosen scale like 1 icon = 5 students.
A bar graph uses equal-width rectangular bars whose heights or lengths read exact counts on a numbered scale.
Raw lists of fifty answers look messy—Organising Data turns chaos into crystal-clear insight.

board.text: Data = facts gathered to learn cleanly

text.en: As you count responses one by one, draw vertical Tally Marks; on the fifth mark, draw a diagonal slash across four to bundle 5 cleanly!
Counting total tally bundles gives the Frequency—how many times each choice appeared.
Want a quick picture chart? Use a Pictograph—repeating a smiley, book or apple icon along rows.

board.text: Pictographs use icons to show counts

text.en: Always check the Legend / Key! If 1 apple icon = 10 trees, then 3 apples mean 30, and half an apple means 5!

board.text: Half icon = half the scale value

text.en: When numbers reach hundreds like 140 or 235, drawing dozens of half-icons gets awkward—switch to a Bar Graph!

board.text: Large counts? Draw a Bar Graph!

text.en: On a Bar Graph, draw one axis with categories and one numbered axis using an even scale like 0, 10, 20, 30.

board.text: Axis scale jumps in equal steps

text.en: Keep every bar the exact same width with equal gaps between bars so your eyes compare heights fairly!
Never start bars clumsily without labelling title, both axes and the scale—clear labels prevent misleading charts.
Remember the pipeline: Raw Data -> Tally & Frequency Table -> Pictograph or Bar Graph for clear decisions!

problem.en: In a school library pictograph, 1 book picture represents 20 borrowed books. Science has 4 book pictures and Maths has 2½ book pictures. How many books were borrowed in each?

why.en: Key: 1 full book picture = 20 books, so ½ picture = 10 books.

prompt.en: Why do bar graphs require every bar to have the same width and start from zero?

requiredIdeas.en: Different bar widths or cut axes make smaller counts look artificially big.
Equal width lets height alone fairly compare quantities.

commonMisconceptions.en: Wider bars look nicer for bigger items.

points.en: Tally marks group counts in bundles of 5.
Frequency = number of times a value occurs.
Pictograph: check the symbol scale and half-symbols.
Bar graph: uniform width, equal spacing, equal axis scale.
